item.text: {"text":"For objective L=ΣₜwₜE[ℓₜ], separately averaging each task’s minibatch gives ĝ=Σₜwₜ mean(∇ℓₜ). With positive fixed counts nₜ and unbiased within-task sampling, E[ĝ]=∇L regardless of allocation: more samples reduce noise without increasing that task’s expected weight. Under independent, with-replacement sampling, Cov(ĝ)=Σₜwₜ²Σₜ/nₜ, where Σₜ is the per-example gradient covariance. Applying stratified-sampling theory, the allocation minimizing covariance trace at fixed total count is nₜ∝|wₜ|√tr(Σₜ). These are direct gradient-estimator deductions from [stratified allocation results](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/12-001-x/2015002/article/14249/02-eng.htm).\n\nRandom counts retain unbiasedness if every task remains present and samples are unbiased conditional on counts; covariance then uses E[1/Nₜ], so count randomness increases variance relative to fixed allocation with the same means. Empty batches change the conclusion: if omitted tasks contribute zero, E[ĝ]=ΣₜwₜP(Nₜ>0)∇Lₜ. For B independent task draws with probabilities pₜ, presence probability is 1−(1−pₜ)ᴮ, attenuating rare tasks. Renormalizing weights over present tasks introduces another random weighting. These formulas follow by conditioning on counts. Unbiased alternatives include guaranteed positive counts, inverse-presence weighting, or the per-draw estimator (wₜ/pₜ)∇ℓₜ, consistent with [importance-weighted SGD](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v37/zhaoa15.html). Thus unchanged separate-mean reduction preserves expected weights only when absence is prevented or corrected; pooled averaging instead weights tasks by allocation. Equal expected raw gradients also do not guarantee equal Adam updates or training trajectories."}
